title: Low-Cost IoT Energy Monitoring for Smart Buildings: A 30-Day Field Study of an ESP32 and PZEM-004T Prototype

authors.name: Rizky Aditya Pratama
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Brawijaya

authors.name: Dewi Anggraini Susanto
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Brawijaya

authors.name: Hendra Wijaya
authors.affiliation: Smart Building Research Group, Universitas Brawijaya

abstract: Mid-sized commercial and academic buildings across Indonesia waste somewhere between 18% and 30% of their electricity, and most of that loss stays invisible until the PLN bill lands at the end of the month. The usual fix, branch-level submetering with commercial smart meters, runs upward of USD 220 per node and rarely ships with a workable cloud path for retrofit projects. We built a low-cost alternative using the ESP32-WROOM-32 paired with the PZEM-004T v3.0 energy sensor, then deployed 12 nodes across the circuit branches of a teaching building at Universitas Brawijaya for 30 straight days. The prototype logged voltage, current, active power, power factor, and accumulated energy at 1 Hz, pushing data over MQTT to a ThingsBoard server. Compared against a Fluke 435-II reference analyzer, voltage error stayed within \b\u00b10.42%\b, current within \b\u00b10.58%\b, and active power within \b\u00b10.65%\b. The MQTT pipeline delivered 99.2% of payloads with a mean end-to-end latency of 187 ms. Total energy logged across the deployment came to 4,832 kWh, and the load profile uncovered a 14.7% reduction opportunity tied to after-hours HVAC behavior. Per-node cost landed at USD 18.40, roughly 8% of the commercial alternative. The work shows that careful sensor calibration, paired with a thin MQTT stack on the ESP32, can deliver utility-grade visibility for retrofit deployments in tropical academic buildings.

content.text: Indonesia's commercial building sector pulled roughly 38% of the country's total electricity in 2023, according to PLN's annual statistical report, and a sizable share of that, somewhere between 18% and 30% depending on building type, simply leaks away through unscheduled HVAC, idle office equipment, and unmonitored auxiliary loads [1], [2]. In Malang, where this work was carried out, most mid-sized academic and office buildings still rely on a single utility-grade meter sitting at the main switchboard. The question that kept coming back to us was unglamorous but stubborn: how do you actually see where the kilowatt-hours go without dropping IDR 30 million on commercial submetering for every panel?

Several research groups have already chipped away at this. Rahman et al. [3] paired an Arduino Mega with three SCT-013 current transformers and reached \u00b11.8% accuracy, but their setup couldn't read voltage natively and skipped power factor entirely. Chen and Liu [4] used an STM32F103 with a custom analog front-end, which hit \u00b10.5% on power but cost USD 67 per node, mostly burned on the analog isolation stage. Saputra et al. [5] built an ESP8266 logger reading PZEM-004T over UART, posting to ThingBoard at 0.2 Hz, and saw 92.4% MQTT delivery on a campus Wi-Fi that wasn't ideal. Park et al. [6] added LoRa as the upstream link but reported 4.3 s end-to-end latency, too slow for fault response. None of these works tested a multi-node deployment for longer than a week, and none reported branch-level cost analysis against commercial alternatives in a tropical building setting.

So the gap isn't hardware existence; it's evidence. There's almost no published, multi-week, multi-branch study showing whether a sub-USD 20 node can actually match a Fluke-class reference instrument over real building loads with their messy harmonics, switching transients, and irregular power factors. The PZEM-004T v3.0 ships with a factory cal certificate, sure, but how does it hold up after 720 continuous hours under tropical humidity and 32 \u00b0C cabinet temperatures? That's the question we wanted answered before recommending the design to facilities teams.

This paper presents a 30-day field study of a 12-node ESP32 + PZEM-004T monitoring system deployed across the teaching building of the Faculty of Engineering at Universitas Brawijaya. Our contributions are:
• A reproducible hardware-firmware design for branch-level energy monitoring at USD 18.40 per node, including BOM and PCB files.
• A calibrated accuracy study against a Fluke 435-II reference, reporting per-channel error across 4,832 kWh of real building consumption.
• A statistical assessment of MQTT delivery and latency over a campus 802.11n network during normal teaching hours.
• A short load-disaggregation analysis showing where the 14.7% identified savings actually live in the load profile.

The rest of the paper is laid out as follows. Section II walks through prior IoT energy monitoring work and the gap we're filling. Section III covers the hardware, calibration procedure, firmware structure, and cloud topology. Section IV reports field results across accuracy, latency, delivery, and cost. Section V wraps up with what worked, what didn't, and three concrete directions we want to chase next.

The literature on building-scale energy monitoring sits at the crossing of three research strands: low-cost instrumentation, embedded IoT communication, and load analytics. We review each in turn, then close with the gap we're targeting. Where useful, we compare papers against each other rather than only against our own work.

Hardware approaches split roughly into two camps: discrete analog front-ends and integrated metering ICs. On the discrete side, Rahman et al. [3] read three SCT-013-030 current transformers through a TL084 op-amp into an Arduino Mega 2560 ADC, sampling at 1.2 kSPS. They reported \u00b11.8% RMS current accuracy on resistive loads, which sounds fine until you note their test bench had only one inductive load, and the calibration drifted 0.7% over a 48-hour soak test. Chen and Liu [4] went the opposite direction with an STM32F103 plus dedicated isolation amplifiers (HCPL-7800), hitting \u00b10.5% on power. Their honest cost breakdown, though, sat at USD 67 per node, and the four-layer PCB they needed for the analog routing isn't reproducible by most undergraduate teams. Park and Kim [7] tried to split the difference with the ADE7758 metering IC behind an STM32, getting \u00b10.3% on a single phase but stopping at lab-bench testing. None of these reached field deployment beyond 72 hours. Saputra et al. [5] picked the PZEM-004T precisely because it sidesteps the analog design problem: the metering IC inside (a Vango V9881D variant) is already certified to \u00b11.0%. Their ESP8266 link, however, dropped to 92.4% delivery during peak campus traffic, which they attributed to single-radio Wi-Fi contention. Mwangi et al. [8] confirmed PZEM-004T's stability over 14 days in a Kenyan office building but only logged at 0.1 Hz, far too coarse for switching event capture. The thread that runs through all of this work: PZEM-004T-class modules deliver acceptable accuracy at a price point that custom analog can't match, but their integration with a proper IoT stack and longer field validation is still thin.

content.Title: Comparative Architecture of Low-Cost Energy Sensing Approaches
content.Prompt: A horizontal three-column comparison diagram titled 'Low-Cost Energy Sensing Architectures'. The leftmost column shows 'Discrete Analog Front-End' with stacked labeled blocks: 'Current Transformer (SCT-013)', 'Op-Amp Signal Conditioning (TL084)', 'External ADC', 'MCU (Arduino Mega)', and at the bottom an annotation reading 'Cost: USD 25-40, Accuracy: \u00b11.8%'. The middle column shows 'Dedicated Metering IC' with blocks 'Shunt + Voltage Divider', 'Isolation Amplifier (HCPL-7800)', 'ADE7758 Metering IC', 'STM32F103 MCU', and annotation 'Cost: USD 50-70, Accuracy: \u00b10.3-0.5%'. The rightmost column, highlighted with a green border, shows 'Integrated Module (this work)' with blocks 'PZEM-004T v3.0 (V9881D inside)', 'UART Bus (Modbus-RTU)', 'ESP32-WROOM-32', 'MQTT Client', and annotation 'Cost: USD 18.40, Accuracy: \u00b10.65%'. Arrows flow downward in each column from sensing to communication. Use a clean, technical drawing style with rectangular blocks, thin black outlines, blue fill for sensors, gray fill for MCUs, and green fill for communication blocks. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 1 lays out the three sensing architectures side by side. What stands out is how the PZEM-004T column collapses several stages of analog design into a single certified module, which is exactly why the BOM cost drops so dramatically. The trade-off is loss of low-level access to raw current waveforms, so harmonic analysis beyond the sensor's onboard computation isn't possible without modification.

On the upstream side, the literature splits between Wi-Fi/MQTT, LoRaWAN, and cellular. Saputra et al. [5] used MQTT over campus Wi-Fi and saw 92.4% delivery, which the authors blamed on QoS-0 in the ESP8266 client and access-point handover during high-density teaching hours. Park et al. [6] swapped to LoRaWAN for a multi-floor deployment and stayed above 99% delivery, but at the cost of a 4.3 s end-to-end latency, more than enough to miss switching transients in HVAC equipment. Anggraini and Hartono [9] tested NB-IoT in a Surabaya office and reported 1.7 s latency with 98.1% delivery, but per-node monthly data costs came to IDR 45,000, which adds up fast across 12 branches. Lin et al. [10] benchmarked QoS-1 MQTT on the ESP32 specifically and found that delivery climbed to 99.4% at the price of a 2.1\u00d7 RAM footprint, manageable on the WROOM-32's 520 KB SRAM. Chen et al. [11] proposed a hybrid Wi-Fi-with-LoRa-fallback stack but never released the source code, which makes replication tough. The collective gap here: most published deployments either stay under a week or stop at single-node testing, so we don't have a clean reference for what 12 simultaneous ESP32 clients do to a campus access point during normal operation.

Once data is flowing, the analytics question takes over. Kelly and Knottenbelt [12] showed that 1 Hz active-power data is enough to disaggregate HVAC, lighting, and plug loads in residential settings using a CNN, hitting 87% F1 on five appliance categories. Their work, though, ran on UK semi-detached houses with stable 50 Hz, single-phase service, conditions that don't match a tropical academic building. Setiawan et al. [13] applied a simpler rule-based disaggregation to PZEM-004T data from a 6-classroom building and recovered 78% of the HVAC load, missing the rest because the chiller pump and AHU drew similar power signatures. Wang and Zhao [14] argued that for retrofit applications, branch-level monitoring beats whole-house disaggregation outright because the labels are already implicit in the wiring, an argument that shaped our decision to instrument 12 separate branches rather than one main feed. Putri et al. [15] reported a 12.4% energy reduction in a Yogyakarta university lab after deploying branch-level visibility and giving facilities staff a daily dashboard, suggesting the savings are real once the data exists. Taken together, the prior work shows three things: branch-level monitoring is more useful than whole-building inference for retrofit; PZEM-004T-class modules can carry the load if calibrated; and no published study has actually combined those two with a 30+ day, 10+ node campus deployment and reported the end-to-end numbers we needed. That's the gap this paper is trying to close.

This section walks through the four design layers of the prototype: the system-level architecture and why we chose each block, the sensing hardware and its calibration against a Fluke reference, the firmware running on each ESP32 node, and the cloud-side data pipeline. The driving constraint throughout was reproducibility. Every part, from the PCB to the ThingsBoard config, had to be something a facilities engineer in Malang could actually rebuild from the paper without specialist gear.

We picked a star topology with twelve sensing nodes reporting independently to a single ThingsBoard server, rather than a mesh or gateway-aggregator scheme. The reasoning was practical: each electrical branch panel in the building already sits within Wi-Fi range of the campus 802.11n network, so adding an aggregator gateway would have been redundant hardware and an extra failure point. Honestly, we considered a LoRaWAN backhaul early on, after reading [6], but the 4.3 s latency they reported would have made it impossible to capture sub-second switching transients on the chiller. Wi-Fi MQTT, even with its delivery hiccups, gives us the millisecond-class visibility we needed for fault detection. Each node is independent: if one drops, the other eleven keep logging. The cloud server runs ThingsBoard Community Edition on a campus VM (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) and handles ingestion, time-series storage in PostgreSQL, and the dashboard.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture of the IoT Energy Monitoring Prototype
content.Prompt: A horizontally-flowing block diagram titled 'IoT Energy Monitoring System Architecture'. On the far left, a rectangular block labeled 'Building Electrical Panel' contains 12 small rounded sub-blocks labeled 'Branch 1' through 'Branch 12' with current-carrying lines drawn through each. From each branch, a thick green arrow labeled 'AC Current/Voltage' flows into a column of 12 sensing nodes, each shown as a stacked pair: a blue rectangle 'PZEM-004T v3.0' on top and an orange rectangle 'ESP32-WROOM-32' below, connected by an arrow labeled 'UART Modbus 9600 bps'. A wireless symbol radiates from each ESP32 with the label 'Wi-Fi 802.11n / MQTT'. All twelve wireless symbols converge into a central cloud-shaped block in the middle labeled 'Campus 802.11n Access Point (Cisco WAP-571)'. From the cloud, a single arrow labeled 'TCP/MQTT QoS-1, port 1883' flows right into a server block labeled 'ThingsBoard Server (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM)' which contains three internal sub-blocks: 'MQTT Broker', 'PostgreSQL TS Store', and 'Dashboard UI'. From the server, two output arrows flow rightward to user-end blocks: 'Web Dashboard' (a monitor icon) and 'REST API' (a code-bracket icon). Above the diagram, label '12 nodes \u00d7 1 Hz = 12 samples/s'. Use clean rectangular blocks with thin black outlines, blue fill for sensors, orange for MCUs, gray for network infrastructure, and green for the server. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the full pipeline. The most important design decision visible here is the absence of a local gateway. Each ESP32 publishes directly to the broker, which means the only single point of failure is the ThingsBoard server itself, and we mitigate that with a 24-hour local SD-card buffer on each node (covered in Section III-D). The 1 Hz sample rate per node was chosen as the lowest rate that still captures HVAC compressor cycling without overwhelming the campus access point.

In (1), $P$ is active power in watts, $V$ is the RMS line voltage in volts, $I$ is the RMS line current in amperes, and $\cos\varphi$ is the displacement power factor between voltage and current waveforms. The PZEM-004T computes all four quantities internally, so the ESP32 simply reads the result over UART. We chose this formulation, rather than computing instantaneous power and integrating, because the PZEM's onboard metering IC samples at 12.8 kSPS, far above what the ESP32 ADC could manage cleanly while also handling MQTT and Wi-Fi tasks.

Each sensing node consists of a custom 50 mm \u00d7 75 mm two-layer PCB carrying an ESP32-WROOM-32, a PZEM-004T v3.0 module with its 100 A split-core CT, a Hi-Link HLK-PM03 isolated 3.3 V power supply, an SD card slot, and an MCP1700 LDO for sensor-side decoupling. The CT clamps onto the line conductor of each branch, and a flying lead taps the line voltage from the busbar through a 250 mA fast-blow fuse. Before deployment, every PZEM-004T module went through a two-point calibration against a Fluke 435-II Power Quality Analyzer, with a 5 kW resistive load bank as the reference and a 3 kW induction motor as the inductive case. Calibration coefficients were stored in the ESP32's NVS flash. Table I summarizes the per-node bill of materials and calibration results.

content.Title: Per-Node Bill of Materials and Calibration Results

content.text: Table I lists the BOM and calibration outcomes. The single biggest cost line is the PZEM-004T at USD 9.80, which is also where the accuracy comes from. We deliberately skipped a 4-layer PCB (would have cost USD 3.80 more per node) because the Fluke comparison showed no benefit at our sample rate. The \u00b10.65% power error sits well inside the IEC 62053-21 Class 2 utility meter spec, which was our acceptance threshold.

content.Title: Calibration Bench Against Fluke 435-II Reference Analyzer
content.Prompt: An annotated photograph-style technical illustration of an electrical calibration bench. At center-left, a 5 kW resistive load bank is shown as a stack of ten coiled heating elements mounted on a vented metal frame, labeled 'Resistive Load Bank 5 kW @ 230 V'. To its right sits a 3 kW three-phase induction motor on a small stand, labeled 'Inductive Reference 3 kW Motor (PF 0.78 lag)'. Both connect through a labeled busbar to two parallel measurement paths: the upper path leads to a yellow Fluke 435-II Power Quality Analyzer with its display visible showing 'V: 226.4 V, I: 21.8 A, P: 4928 W, PF: 0.998', labeled 'Reference Instrument'. The lower path leads to the prototype node, shown as a transparent enclosure containing a labeled PZEM-004T module (white rectangle with terminals), an ESP32 dev board (green rectangle with USB), and a CT clamp (split blue ring around the live conductor), with a small label 'Device Under Test'. A laptop on the right shows a logging window with timestamped readings. Add small annotation arrows pointing to: 'CT clamp position', 'Voltage tap point through 250 mA fuse', 'UART link to ESP32', and 'Calibration coefficient stored in NVS'. Use clean technical illustration style with realistic component proportions, soft gray shading for metal parts, color-coded wiring (red live, blue neutral, green ground). White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: The firmware runs on FreeRTOS with three pinned tasks. Task A polls the PZEM-004T at 1 Hz over UART using the Modbus-RTU protocol on a 9600 bps link, requesting the six registers covering V, I, P, energy, frequency, and power factor in a single 8-byte query. Task B handles MQTT publishing at QoS-1 to the ThingsBoard broker, with exponential backoff on connection failure (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, capped at 60 s). Task C manages the SD-card buffer, which fills with line-delimited JSON records whenever the MQTT publish queue exceeds a 50-record threshold, and drains back through MQTT once connectivity returns. The buffer holds up to 86,400 records (24 hours at 1 Hz) before it starts overwriting. The measurement error percentage we report against the Fluke reference uses the standard relative-error formulation, given in (2).

In (2), $\varepsilon$ is the relative measurement error in percent, $X_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the value reported by the prototype node, and $X_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding value from the Fluke 435-II analyzer at the same timestamp. We compute $\varepsilon$ separately for voltage, current, active power, and power factor, then take the RMS error across a 60-minute calibration window. This matches the procedure in IEC 62053-21 Annex B, which let us compare against the Class 2 meter threshold directly.

content.Title: Firmware Task Flowchart on the ESP32 Node
content.Prompt: A vertical flowchart titled 'ESP32 Firmware Tasks (FreeRTOS, 3 pinned tasks)' showing three parallel column flows. Column 1 'Task A: Sensor Poll (Core 0, 1 Hz)' starts with a rounded green capsule 'START', flows to a rectangle 'Build Modbus query (8 bytes)', then 'Send via UART2 @ 9600 bps', then a diamond 'CRC valid?', with NO branch flowing to 'Log error, retry x3' and YES branch to 'Parse 6 registers (V,I,P,E,f,PF)', then 'Push to RAM ring buffer', then 'Delay 1000 ms', looping back to the build query block. Column 2 'Task B: MQTT Publisher (Core 1, async)' starts with 'START', flows to 'Read ring buffer', diamond 'Wi-Fi connected?', NO leads to 'Backoff 1s\u21922s\u21924s\u2192...\u219260s' looping, YES leads to 'Publish QoS-1 to ThingsBoard topic', diamond 'PUBACK received <500ms?', NO to 'Increment failure counter', YES to 'Mark record as sent', looping back. Column 3 'Task C: SD Buffer (Core 0, event-triggered)' starts with 'START', flows to a diamond 'Queue depth > 50?', NO to 'Idle/wait', YES to 'Append JSON to /buffer.log on SD', then diamond 'Wi-Fi back online?', YES to 'Replay records via MQTT', then 'Truncate sent rows', looping back. Use rectangular process boxes with thin black outlines, diamond decision shapes in light yellow, rounded green capsules for start, rounded red capsules for error states. Add labels 'Stack: 8 KB', 'Stack: 12 KB', 'Stack: 4 KB' at the top of each column. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 4 shows the three FreeRTOS tasks. The most subtle design choice, and the one that took the most iteration, was pinning Task A and Task C to Core 0 while leaving Task B (the heavy MQTT/Wi-Fi work) on Core 1. Mixing them on the same core caused 200\u2013400 ms jitter in the sensor poll timing, which threw off the 1 Hz cadence. Once split, jitter dropped below 8 ms, well within tolerance for our analysis.

On the server side, ThingsBoard receives each MQTT publish on a per-device topic of the form v1/devices/me/telemetry, with a JSON payload carrying the six metered values plus a node ID and timestamp. A rule chain inside ThingsBoard tags each record with the branch label (e.g., 'AHU-Floor2', 'Lighting-Floor3-Wing-A') and writes it to PostgreSQL with a 90-day retention policy, after which records roll into a compressed cold-storage table. We picked PostgreSQL over the more common Cassandra backend because the 12-node, 1 Hz workload tops out at roughly 1.04 million rows per day, well inside what a single-node Postgres instance handles comfortably. The dashboard aggregates to 1-minute averages for live views and 15-minute averages for the daily report. For the round-trip latency analysis in Section IV, we time-stamp at publish on the ESP32 (using NTP-synced time) and at insert on the server, then take the difference.

content.Prompt:
A horizontal layered diagram titled 'End-to-End Data Pipeline with Latency Annotations' showing five labeled stages connected by left-to-right arrows. Stage 1 'Sensor Read' is a blue block labeled 'PZEM-004T → ESP32 (UART 9600 bps)' with timing annotation '~85 ms'. Stage 2 'JSON Build + MQTT Publish' is an orange block labeled 'cJSON encode + MQTT QoS-1 to broker' with annotation '~12 ms'. Stage 3 'Wi-Fi to AP' is a gray block with a wireless icon labeled '802.11n campus WAP' with annotation '~25 ms (avg)'. Stage 4 'TCP to ThingsBoard' is a gray block labeled 'TCP port 1883 over campus VLAN' with annotation '~38 ms'. Stage 5 'Rule Chain + DB Insert' is a green block labeled 'ThingsBoard rule chain → PostgreSQL TS table' with annotation '~27 ms'. Below each block, a horizontal timeline bar shows the cumulative latency, growing from 85 ms after stage 1 to 187 ms after stage 5. At the right edge, a final summary box reads 'Mean RTT: 187 ms
P95: 312 ms
P99: 547 ms
Delivery: 99.2%'. Above the diagram, draw a small clock icon with label 'NTP sync ±5 ms (id.pool.ntp.org)'. Use clean rectangular blocks with thin black outlines, color-coded by stage type, with timeline bars in a light gradient. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 5 traces a single data point from sensor read to database row, with measured latency contributions at each step. The dominant component is the sensor read itself at roughly 85 ms, set by the Modbus baud rate, which we couldn't shrink without abandoning the PZEM's documented protocol. The Wi-Fi and TCP stages combine to about 63 ms in the median case but balloon to over 400 ms during the morning class transition periods, when the access point handles the largest user load.

We deployed twelve nodes across the teaching building of the Faculty of Engineering at Universitas Brawijaya from 1 March to 30 March 2024, covering 30 consecutive days that spanned regular classes, mid-term exams, and a national holiday. Total data captured: 31,104,000 sensor readings (12 nodes \u00d7 1 Hz \u00d7 86,400 s/day \u00d7 30 days) before any drop. We analyze accuracy against the Fluke 435-II reference, MQTT delivery and latency, comparison with prior work, and reliability under normal building conditions.

Twelve nodes were installed in the main electrical room of Engineering Building A, each clamping onto a single branch breaker output. Branch labels covered: three HVAC branches (chiller, two AHUs), three lighting branches (ground, second, third floors), three power-outlet branches per floor, one server-room branch, one elevator, and one general utility. Reference measurements with the Fluke 435-II were taken on six randomly selected branches during three 60-minute calibration windows (one in week 1, one in week 2, one in week 4) to track drift. Ambient cabinet temperature ranged from 26 \u00b0C overnight to 33 \u00b0C during peak afternoon load, recorded by a DHT22 inside one of the enclosures. Wi-Fi was the campus 802.11n network on a Cisco WAP-571 access point in the same room, shared with no other heavy clients during off-hours but loaded with up to 40 student devices during class transitions.

content.Title: Field Deployment Configuration and Test Parameters

content.text: Table II captures the field configuration. The 30-day window was chosen long enough to cover at least one full HVAC maintenance cycle and short enough to fit the academic calendar before exams disrupted the load profile. The three-window calibration schedule was a compromise between thoroughness and the disruption that pulling the Fluke onto live branches caused for facilities staff.

content.text: Across the three calibration windows, voltage RMS error came in at \u00b10.42%, current at \u00b10.58%, and active power at \u00b10.65%. That last number is what mattered most for our application, and it sits comfortably below the 1.0% IEC 62053-21 Class 1 boundary (and the 2.0% Class 2 acceptance threshold we set going in). The frequency channel was effectively perfect at \u00b10.04 Hz, which makes sense because the PZEM-004T derives it from the same internal clock that drives its sampling. Power factor showed the largest spread at \u00b10.018 absolute, with the worst readings clustered around the chiller branch, where high inductive distortion and switching transients produced the messiest waveforms. Total energy logged across all 12 branches over the 30 days came to 4,832 kWh, against a Fluke-derived reference of 4,801 kWh, a discrepancy of 0.65% that tracks precisely with the per-sample power error. Notice that no error compounding showed up over time, which is what you'd hope for if the calibration is genuinely stable rather than just lucky.

Table III summarizes ten metrics we tracked. Every channel cleared its target, but two are worth pausing on. The 99.2% MQTT delivery rate is high, but the 0.8% loss isn't randomly distributed, it concentrates between 07:30 and 08:15 on weekdays, which lines up exactly with the morning class transition when the AP load spikes. And the latency P95 of 312 ms versus a mean of 187 ms tells you the distribution has a fat right tail, which we'll come back to in the discussion.

content.Title: Per-Channel Measurement Error Across Three Calibration Windows
content.Prompt: A grouped vertical bar chart titled 'Measurement Error vs. Fluke 435-II Reference Across Calibration Windows'. The x-axis shows five categories in this order: 'Voltage', 'Current', 'Active Power', 'Frequency (\u00d710 Hz)', 'Power Factor (\u00d7100)'. The y-axis shows 'Relative RMS Error (%)' from 0 to 1.2, with gridlines every 0.2. For each x-axis category, three side-by-side bars are shown representing the three calibration windows: 'Week 1' (light blue), 'Week 2' (medium blue), 'Week 4' (dark blue). Bar heights are: Voltage W1=0.41, W2=0.43, W4=0.42; Current W1=0.55, W2=0.59, W4=0.60; Active Power W1=0.62, W2=0.66, W4=0.67; Frequency W1=0.04, W2=0.05, W4=0.04; Power Factor W1=1.7, W2=1.8, W4=1.8 (note: PF scaled \u00d7100 for visibility). Each bar has its numeric value printed above it. A horizontal red dashed line at y=1.0 is labeled 'IEC 62053-21 Class 1 boundary'. A horizontal green dashed line at y=2.0 is labeled 'Class 2 boundary' but is above the chart top so visible only at the legend. A legend in the upper-right shows 'Week 1', 'Week 2', 'Week 4' with their colors and a note 'n=60 min per window per channel'. Title at the top reads 'Measurement Error vs. Fluke 435-II Reference'. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 7 plots per-channel error across the three calibration windows. What's actually striking is the lack of drift, every bar in week 4 sits within 0.05% of its week 1 counterpart. We expected to see some thermal creep on the current channel given the 33 \u00b0C peak cabinet temperatures, but it never showed up at the resolution we could measure. The PZEM's internal temperature compensation is doing real work here.

In (3), $\eta$ is the MQTT delivery rate in percent, $N_{\mathrm{success}}$ is the count of payloads that received PUBACK from the broker within the 5-second QoS-1 timeout, and $N_{\mathrm{total}}$ is the total publish attempts in the measurement window. Across the 30 days, we measured $N_{\mathrm{total}} = 31{,}104{,}000$ and $N_{\mathrm{success}} = 30{,}855{,}168$, yielding $\eta = 99.2\%$.

How does the prototype stack up against published alternatives? Table IV puts it next to the three closest comparators. Method A [4] uses an STM32 with a dedicated metering IC and reaches \u00b10.5% on power, slightly better than ours, but at USD 67 per node and only seven days of testing. Method B [8] is a PZEM-004T with ESP8266 from a Kenyan deployment, similar accuracy at \u00b10.7% but with a 0.1 Hz sample rate that misses fast switching events entirely. Method C [9] uses NB-IoT and reports \u00b10.4% accuracy but with a USD 31 hardware cost and recurring data charges. The 6.2 percentage-point gap between our 99.2% delivery and the 92.4% reported by Saputra et al. [5] is the most interesting comparison because we use almost identical hardware on the sensor side. We tracked the difference back to two things: their ESP8266 only has a single radio task that contends with the application, while the ESP32's dual-core scheduling lets MQTT live on its own core, and they used QoS-0 while we used QoS-1 with retry. We tested this hypothesis directly by reflashing two of our nodes with QoS-0 firmware for 24 hours, and delivery dropped to 94.7%, almost exactly Saputra's number.

content.Title: Comparison with Related Energy Monitoring Systems

content.text: Table IV makes the trade-off pretty plain. Pure power accuracy isn't where we win, [4] and [9] both edge us there. What this work delivers is the longest field validation in the comparison set (30 days vs. 7\u201314), the most nodes (12 vs. 1\u20138), the lowest hardware cost without recurring fees, and the only one with an explicit QoS comparison and per-window calibration drift analysis. For retrofit deployments where the question is 'will this still work three weeks from now', that combination matters more than the third decimal place of accuracy.

content.Title: Cost vs. Power Accuracy Comparison Across Reviewed Systems
content.Prompt: A 2D scatter plot titled 'Cost vs. Power Accuracy Across Energy Monitoring Systems'. The x-axis is 'Power Accuracy Error (%)' from 0.3 to 1.0, lower is better. The y-axis is 'Per-Node Cost (USD)' from 15 to 75, lower is better. The plot has gridlines every 0.1 on x and every 10 on y. Five data points are plotted as colored circles with labels: (1) at x=0.5, y=67, color red, label 'Chen & Liu [4] STM32+ADE7758', (2) at x=0.9, y=21.5, color orange, label 'Saputra et al. [5] ESP8266', (3) at x=0.7, y=19.2, color yellow, label 'Mwangi et al. [8] ESP32', (4) at x=0.4, y=31, color blue, label 'Anggraini & Hartono [9] NB-IoT', (5) at x=0.65, y=18.4, color GREEN with a thicker outline and a star marker, label 'This work (12 nodes, 30 days)'. Each point has a small text label adjacent to it. The lower-left corner is shaded light green and labeled 'Best zone (low cost + low error)'. The upper-right corner is shaded light red and labeled 'Worst zone'. A diagonal dashed gray line from upper-left to lower-right represents 'cost-accuracy frontier'. Add a legend in the upper-right showing the marker colors mapped to system names. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Reliability over the 30 days came down to two questions: did any nodes fail, and how did the system handle the campus power outage that hit the building on 18 March? On node hardware, eleven of twelve nodes ran the entire 30 days uninterrupted. Node 7, which sat on the elevator branch, rebooted three times, all of them traced to a brownout when the elevator started under load (the HLK-PM03 supply is rated for 230 VAC \u00b115%, and the bus dropped to 191 V transiently). We added a 470 \u03bcF bulk capacitor on the supply input for the production version, but the deployed nodes kept their original wiring, so the failures show up honestly in the data. During the 18 March outage (47 minutes, 13:42\u201314:29), all twelve nodes failed over to SD-card buffering and replayed their data once power returned. Replay completed within 6 minutes for the slowest node, with zero records lost. The load profile across the building showed a distinct overnight baseline of 8.4 kW that we didn't expect, almost all of it from a single branch (one of the AHUs that wasn't being scheduled off after hours). Killing that single overnight cycle would save roughly 14.7% of total building consumption, which we flagged to facilities as the headline finding.

content.Title: Reliability and Robustness Test Outcomes
Rows: All 12 nodes buffered to SD; full replay

content.text: Table V lists the reliability events we tracked. The most informative one was the building outage on 18 March, because it tested the SD-buffer-and-replay path that we couldn't easily simulate in the lab. All twelve nodes recovered, but the slowest replay took 6 minutes against the broker, which suggests we should look at parallel replay with rate limiting if a deployment scales beyond about 30 nodes.

content.Title: Building Load Profile Over a Representative Week with Outage Event
content.Prompt: A multi-line time-series chart titled 'Total Building Active Power, Week of 13-19 March 2024'. The x-axis spans 7 days from 'Mon 13 Mar 00:00' to 'Sun 19 Mar 23:59', with day-of-week labels at midnight gridlines. The y-axis shows 'Active Power (kW)' from 0 to 60, with gridlines every 10 kW. Three colored lines are plotted: a dark blue line labeled 'Total (sum of 12 branches)' with a typical workday profile rising from 8 kW overnight to 47 kW during the day, dropping to 8 kW overnight again, peak around 12:00-14:00 each day; a green line labeled 'HVAC (chiller + 2 AHUs)' that tracks roughly half the total during work hours and stays at a constant 6 kW overnight (the unwanted AHU cycle); an orange line labeled 'Lighting + Outlets + Server' that holds steady around 8 kW during day, drops to 2 kW overnight. On 18 March (Monday of the second week), a vertical red dashed line is drawn at 13:42 labeled 'Outage start', and another vertical red dashed line at 14:29 labeled 'Outage end (47 min)'. Between these two lines, all three traces are shown as a flat gap (no data from the building). After the outage ends, a small annotation arrow points to a thin dashed segment labeled 'SD-buffer replay (6 min)' showing the gap being filled retroactively. The weekend (16-17 March) shows a much lower profile, peaking around 18 kW. Above the chart, a horizontal annotation bar reads 'Peak observed: 47.3 kW @ Wed 14:18' with an arrow pointing to that exact data point. A legend in the upper-right shows the three line colors and labels. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: We built and deployed a 12-node IoT energy monitoring system using ESP32-WROOM-32 and PZEM-004T v3.0 modules across the teaching building of the Faculty of Engineering at Universitas Brawijaya, then tracked it for 30 consecutive days. Against a Fluke 435-II reference, the prototype held \u00b10.42% on voltage, \u00b10.58% on current, and \u00b10.65% on active power, all of which sit inside the IEC 62053-21 Class 1 boundary. The MQTT pipeline carried 99.2% of payloads with a mean end-to-end latency of 187 ms, the system survived a 47-minute power outage with zero data loss, and per-node hardware cost came to USD 18.40, roughly 8% of the commercial alternative we benchmarked against. The load profile data also surfaced a 14.7% reduction opportunity tied to one AHU that wasn't being scheduled off overnight, which the facilities team has since acted on.

There are limits we don't want to paper over. The PZEM-004T can't expose raw current waveforms, so harmonic analysis beyond what its onboard IC computes is impossible without modifying the module. The 1 Hz sample rate misses transient events shorter than about 500 ms, which means fast capacitor switching or motor inrush won't show up cleanly. The campus 802.11n network handled 12 nodes comfortably, but we don't have evidence that it scales to, say, 100 nodes across multiple buildings without contention issues. And one node (the elevator branch) needed a brownout-recovery patch that didn't make it into the deployed firmware.

Three follow-on directions look most useful from where we sit now. First, replacing the PZEM-004T with a Vango V9881D module on a custom carrier board would expose raw waveform access and let us run per-cycle harmonic analysis at the cost of about USD 4 more per node, worth testing. Second, scaling the deployment to the full Faculty of Engineering complex (roughly 80 branches across four buildings) will stress the broker and the campus AP infrastructure in ways our 12-node test didn't, so a controlled rollout with throughput logging is the next step. Third, layering a lightweight ML model (we're looking at a 1D CNN small enough to run on the ESP32 itself) on top of the 1 Hz active-power stream could push event-level disaggregation onto the edge and cut MQTT bandwidth by an order of magnitude. The hardest part of all of this, honestly, won't be the algorithms; it'll be convincing facilities that the data is worth acting on every day, not just when the bill arrives.
